text.p: Russia should give a firm commitment to clamp down on multi-million-dollar record piracy before it can join the World Trade Organisation, the record industry has told the European Union's external trade chief.

"It is very important that the EU does not facilitate Russia'a accession to WTO without having obtained a firm commitment from the Russian authorities that these and other problems will be effectively dealt with," the record industry lobby IFPI said in a letter to Sir Leon Brittan.

The International Federation of the Phonographic Industry wants Brittan to raise what it calls "rampant piracy of European music in Russia" during a three-day visit to Moscow from Sunday to discuss Moscow's ambitions to join the fair trade watchdog.

The IFPI, which groups industry majors like PolyGram, BMG and EMI, alleges that Russia is the largest pirate market in the world -- accounting for 70 percent of a young but growing market since the country moved to a market economy.
The industry estimates its losses at $300 million and says turnover could more than double if piracy was controlled.

An IFPI report on the Russian industry says the pirate market, often most visible at large flea markets in bigger cities which can make up to $1 million in a weekend, is made up mainly of music cassettes.
But it also acts as a major distribution centre towards the Baltic States and the rest of Europe of pirated compact discs manufactured in Bulgaria and China.
Irina Savelyeva, Head of the IFPI's Moscow office, told reporters in Brussels recently the trade was operated by organised gangsters who use the music money for drugs money.
In one case highlighted by the IFPI report a raid of the Sofia to Moscow train revealed three carriages packed with 50,000 compact discs hidden behind seats, and under panels on the floor.
"Train conductors, as well as the criminals disguised as tourists, had the CDs in their luggage," it said.
